questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Bacterial structure, growth, genetics & antimicrobial resistance
questions.stem: The principal component of the Gram-positive bacterial cell wall is:
options: A thick peptidoglycan layer with teichoic acid
questions.concept: Gram-positive organisms have a thick peptidoglycan layer with teichoic acid that retains the crystal violet-iodine complex. Gram-negative bacteria have thin peptidoglycan with an outer membrane containing endotoxic lipopolysaccharide.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan & Paniker Microbiology 11e, Morphology of Bacteria

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Bacterial structure, growth, genetics & antimicrobial resistance
questions.stem: Bacterial endotoxin differs from exotoxin in that it is:
options: Lipopolysaccharide, heat stable, poorly immunogenic and cannot be toxoided
questions.concept: Endotoxin is the lipid A of the Gram-negative outer membrane, released on lysis, heat stable and causing fever, hypotension and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Exotoxins are secreted proteins, highly potent, antigenic and convertible to toxoids for vaccines.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Bacterial structure, growth, genetics & antimicrobial resistance
questions.stem: Transduction in bacterial genetics refers to transfer of genetic material by:
options: Direct cell-to-cell contact through a pilus
questions.concept: Transduction uses a bacteriophage vector, conjugation requires cell contact via a sex pilus transferring plasmids, and transformation is uptake of free DNA. Conjugation is the most important mechanism for spreading multidrug resistance.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Bacterial structure, growth, genetics & antimicrobial resistance
questions.stem: Methicillin resistance in Staphylococcus aureus is mediated by:
options: The mecA gene encoding an altered penicillin-binding protein PBP2a
questions.concept: PBP2a has low affinity for all beta-lactams, so MRSA is resistant to the entire class including cephalosporins, and requires vancomycin, linezolid or daptomycin. It is detected by cefoxitin disc testing.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Bacterial structure, growth, genetics & antimicrobial resistance
questions.stem: Extended spectrum beta-lactamase producing organisms are best treated with:
questions.concept: ESBLs hydrolyse penicillins and third-generation cephalosporins including aztreonam but are inhibited by clavulanate; carbapenems are the drugs of choice. Carbapenemase producers such as NDM-1 require colistin or newer agents.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Bacterial structure, growth, genetics & antimicrobial resistance
questions.stem: Bacterial spores are formed by:
options: Bacillus and Clostridium species, conferring extreme resistance to heat and disinfectants
questions.concept: Endospores of the aerobic Bacillus and anaerobic Clostridium contain dipicolinic acid and calcium, resisting boiling and most disinfectants, so autoclaving at 121 degrees for 15 minutes is required. Spore destruction is the benchmark of sterilisation.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan & Paniker Microbiology 11e, Morphology of Bacteria

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Bacterial structure, growth, genetics & antimicrobial resistance
questions.stem: The bacterial growth curve phase in which cells are most susceptible to antibiotics is:
questions.concept: Actively dividing cells in log phase are most vulnerable, particularly to cell wall active agents which require ongoing peptidoglycan synthesis. This is why beta-lactams are ineffective against dormant persisters.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Bacterial structure, growth, genetics & antimicrobial resistance
questions.stem: Plasmids differ from bacterial chromosomes in that they:
options: Are extrachromosomal, self-replicating and non-essential for survival
questions.concept: Plasmids carry accessory genes for antibiotic resistance, toxin production and virulence, replicating independently and transferable by conjugation - the principal vehicle for the spread of multidrug resistance.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Bacterial structure, growth, genetics & antimicrobial resistance
questions.stem: The minimum inhibitory concentration is defined as:
options: The lowest antibiotic concentration that prevents visible bacterial growth
questions.concept: MIC defines susceptibility, while the minimum bactericidal concentration is the lowest concentration killing 99.9% of the inoculum. When MBC greatly exceeds MIC the organism is tolerant.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Bacterial structure, growth, genetics & antimicrobial resistance
questions.stem: Quorum sensing in bacteria refers to:
options: Density-dependent regulation of gene expression through signalling molecules
questions.concept: Bacteria secrete autoinducers whose concentration reflects population density, coordinating expression of virulence factors and biofilm formation once a threshold is reached - a target for novel anti-virulence therapies.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Tetanus toxin (tetanospasmin) acts by:
options: Blocking release of the inhibitory neurotransmitters glycine and GABA from Renshaw cells
questions.concept: Tetanospasmin travels retrogradely up motor axons to the spinal cord, cleaving synaptobrevin and preventing inhibitory neurotransmitter release, so unopposed motor activity causes trismus, risus sardonicus and opisthotonus.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Botulinum toxin causes paralysis by:
options: Preventing release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction
questions.concept: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins blocking acetylcholine exocytosis, causing descending flaccid paralysis with diplopia, dysphagia and respiratory failure - the mirror image of tetanus which blocks inhibition.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Infant botulism differs from foodborne botulism in that it results from:
options: Ingestion of spores, often in honey, which germinate in the immature gut
questions.concept: The infant colon lacks a protective flora, so ingested spores germinate and produce toxin in situ, causing a floppy infant with constipation, poor feeding and ptosis. Honey should not be given under one year.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Gas gangrene is most commonly caused by:
options: Clostridium perfringens type A with its alpha toxin (lecithinase)
questions.concept: Alpha toxin is a lecithinase that destroys cell membranes causing myonecrosis, crepitus from gas production and profound toxaemia. The Nagler reaction demonstrates lecithinase activity on egg yolk agar.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Management of established gas gangrene centres on:
options: Urgent radical surgical debridement with high-dose penicillin and supportive care
questions.concept: Extensive debridement or amputation of all necrotic tissue is life-saving because antibiotics cannot penetrate dead tissue; penicillin with clindamycin, which suppresses toxin synthesis, and hyperbaric oxygen are adjuncts.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Prophylaxis for tetanus in a contaminated wound in an incompletely immunised patient requires:
options: Human tetanus immunoglobulin plus tetanus toxoid at separate sites
questions.concept: Passive immunity from immunoglobulin gives immediate protection while toxoid induces active immunity; they must be given with separate syringes at separate sites. Thorough wound toilet remains essential.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Clostridioides difficile causes pseudomembranous colitis chiefly after:
options: Broad-spectrum antibiotic use disrupting the normal colonic flora
questions.concept: Clindamycin, cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones are classic precipitants. Toxins A and B damage the mucosa producing yellow pseudomembranous plaques; diagnosis is by toxin or GDH antigen detection with PCR.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Bacteroides fragilis is clinically important because it is:
options: The commonest anaerobe isolated from intra-abdominal sepsis, and is resistant to penicillin
questions.concept: Bacteroides fragilis is a Gram-negative anaerobic bacillus of the colonic flora causing intra-abdominal and pelvic abscesses. It produces beta-lactamase, so metronidazole, carbapenems or beta-lactam-inhibitor combinations are used.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: The most reliable clinical feature distinguishing tetanus from strychnine poisoning is:
options: Persistent trismus with sustained rigidity between spasms in tetanus
questions.concept: In tetanus muscles remain rigid between spasms and trismus is characteristic, whereas in strychnine poisoning the patient relaxes completely between convulsions. Both preserve consciousness, which is a cruel feature of tetanus.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Anaerobic infections are typically suspected when there is:
options: Foul-smelling discharge with gas in tissues and failure to grow on aerobic culture
questions.concept: Putrid odour from short-chain fatty acids, gas in tissues, necrosis, proximity to mucosal surfaces and sterile pus on routine culture all suggest anaerobes, requiring special transport media and anaerobic culture.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: The characteristic feature of all herpesviruses is:
options: Ability to establish lifelong latency with periodic reactivation
questions.concept: Herpesviruses are enveloped DNA viruses that persist lifelong - HSV and VZV in sensory ganglia, EBV in B lymphocytes, CMV in monocytes - reactivating with stress, immunosuppression or ageing.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Multinucleated giant cells with intranuclear inclusions on a Tzanck smear indicate:
options: Herpes simplex or varicella zoster infection
questions.concept: The Tzanck smear from a fresh vesicle base shows ballooning degeneration with multinucleate giant cells and Cowdry type A intranuclear inclusions, present in both HSV and VZV, so it cannot distinguish between them.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Herpes simplex encephalitis characteristically involves:
options: The temporal lobes, causing haemorrhagic necrosis
questions.concept: HSV-1 encephalitis produces temporal lobe haemorrhagic necrosis with fever, behavioural change, aphasia and seizures. It is the commonest sporadic fatal encephalitis; CSF PCR is diagnostic and intravenous acyclovir must be started empirically.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Shingles (herpes zoster) results from:
options: Reactivation of latent varicella zoster virus in a dorsal root ganglion
questions.concept: Reactivation produces a painful dermatomal vesicular rash that does not cross the midline. Ophthalmic zoster with Hutchinson sign threatens sight, and postherpetic neuralgia is the commonest complication in the elderly.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein-Barr virus is characterised by:
options: Fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy with atypical lymphocytes and a positive Paul-Bunnell test
questions.concept: EBV infects B cells via CD21; the atypical lymphocytes (Downey cells) are reactive T cells. Ampicillin given in error produces a florid maculopapular rash, and splenic rupture is a feared complication.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Epstein-Barr virus is aetiologically linked to all EXCEPT:
questions.concept: EBV is associated with Burkitt and Hodgkin lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder. Kaposi sarcoma is caused by human herpesvirus 8.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Owl's eye intranuclear inclusions are characteristic of:
questions.concept: CMV produces markedly enlarged cells with a large basophilic intranuclear inclusion surrounded by a clear halo. It causes congenital infection with periventricular calcification and deafness, and retinitis in advanced HIV.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: The commonest cause of congenital infection worldwide is:
questions.concept: Congenital CMV affects 0.5 to 1% of live births and is the leading infectious cause of sensorineural deafness and neurodevelopmental disability, though most infected newborns are asymptomatic at birth.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Roseola infantum (exanthem subitum) with high fever followed by rash as the fever settles is caused by:
questions.concept: HHV-6 causes three to five days of high fever in infants, often with febrile convulsions, followed by a maculopapular rash appearing as the temperature falls - the sequence that distinguishes it from measles.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: The drug of choice for cytomegalovirus retinitis in AIDS is:
questions.concept: CMV thymidine kinase differs from that of HSV, so acyclovir is ineffective; ganciclovir, valganciclovir, foscarnet and cidofovir are used. Bone marrow suppression limits ganciclovir and nephrotoxicity limits foscarnet.
